title: Does Your Baby Need a Book on Coding?
author: @NewYorker
content:
If your idea of a perfect board book for people under the age of three is Sandra Boynton’s 1982 classic “Moo, Baa, La La La!,” you might be surprised to discover what’s passing for toddler literature these days. Forget the silly animal high jinks, the humble slapstick of peekaboo and patty-cake, and the earnest overviews of shapes, colors, and numbers; some of today’s baby books have far loftier ambitions. A sampling of titles from the past decade: “Bath Time Physics,” “General Relativity for Babies,” “Baby Loves Aerospace Engineering!,” “Baby Loves Thermodynamics!,” “Baby Loves Quarks!”

Open the sturdy turquoise cover of Ruth Spiro’s “Baby Loves Coding!,” illustrated by Irene Chan, and you might be lulled into thinking that this is, indeed, a book for very young children. It’s small (about seven inches square), short (only ten spreads), made of chunky cardboard, and full of bright colors. It starts off promisingly, with a smiling toy train rolling toward a bobbleheaded, pink-cheeked baby. The text reads:

CHOO CHOO!Here comes the train!

So far, so good. But, over the next few pages, as Baby walks from rug to toy box, we hurtle into strange new territory:

This pattern of stepsis called an algorithm.

The train follows an algorithm, too.A tiny computer tells the trainwhat to do.

Uh-oh.

A programmer writes an algorithmin a language the computercan understand.

The language is called code.The computer reads the code andfollows the steps in the algorithm.

Baby has a headache.

Lately, these tech-oriented books for infants and toddlers seem to be everywhere. The twenty-six books in Spiro’s “Baby Loves Science” series are rivalled by Chris Ferrie’s extensive “Baby University” collection, with such winning titles as “Electromagnetism for Babies,” “Quantum Computing for Babies” (co-authored by William Hurley), and “Robotics for Babies” (co-authored by Sarah Kaiser). And let’s not forget the “Big Science for Tiny Tots” series, from MIT Kids Press, featuring “High Chair Chemistry” and “Playtime Engineering.” In a manic burst of science geekery, there are even special holiday versions of Spiro’s “Baby Loves Science” books, though you might have trouble getting past the word-salad titles: “Baby Loves Angular Momentum on Hanukkah!” and “Baby Loves Photosynthesis on St. Patrick’s Day!.”

Even the publishers seem to realize that all this might be a bit much. The Penguin Random House web page for Spiro’s board books begins, “With tongue firmly in cheek, the Baby Loves Science series introduces highly intellectual science concepts to the littlest learners.” Do babies understand “tongue in cheek”? Even if they do, there’s nothing particularly funny about these books (unless you count Chan’s illustrations of insouciant babies cheerfully absorbing scientific concepts that might mystify a graduate student). Still, at least Spiro’s board books offer the hint of a story, many of them starting with a baby in a familiar setting—a bedroom, a playground, a park—who encounters something in his or her everyday world (for example, a bird) that sparks a treatise on a complex scientific topic (aerospace engineering). Ferrie’s “Baby University” books pay no lip service to character or plot. They contain mini-lectures for babies, with lines like “Mass warps space” and “The forward force is called thrust.”

There’s a mind-numbing, pedantic quality to this language. The brainiest baby books attempt to explain complex scientific concepts—do you know what a quark is? I didn’t, until I read the relevant baby book—in the span of a few pages, with no effort to use words that a toddler would understand. Even a verifiable baby genius couldn’t make sense of lines such as “Protons and neutrons stick together to make a nucleus,” and “The center of a black hole is called a singularity,” and “Air trapped inside a bubble rushes out through a spot made weak by evaporation.” Yet, in the decade or so since STEM-focussed board books first began appearing on the scene, Spiro’s series has sold more than a million copies, and Ferrie’s more than four million. What are we to make of this trend?

Alana Bennison, a children’s librarian at the C. H. Booth Library, in Newtown, Connecticut, credits the books’ popularity to the same parental anxiety that fuelled the Baby Einstein craze in the late nineteen-nineties and early two-thousands. “Parents want to give their children a leg up,” she told me. “They feel tremendous pressure.” The multimedia Baby Einstein franchise, launched, in 1996, by a former high-school English and art teacher who had recently had her first child, included videocassettes, DVDs, flash cards, toys, and board books designed to educate infants and toddlers by immersing them in classical music, major works of art, and words from seven different languages.

By the time it was acquired by the Walt Disney Company, in 2001, Baby Einstein was generating more than seventeen million dollars a year in sales, and over the next few years that number grew to a whopping two hundred million dollars a year. But then Disney started to get hit with complaints, as parents discovered that Baby Einstein had failed to turn their babies into Einsteins. Alarmingly, a 2007 study in The Journal of Pediatrics had found that, for each hour per day spent watching so-called educational baby videos, infants understood, on average, six to eight words fewer than infants who did not watch them—a testament to the essential role of social interaction in early learning. In 2009, after the advocacy group Campaign for a Commercial-Free Childhood threatened a class-action lawsuit over deceptive marketing claims, Disney began offering every household a refund for up to four Baby Einstein DVDs.

If the Baby Einstein products were meant to introduce babies to high culture, from the music of Beethoven and Mozart to the art of da Vinci and van Gogh, many of the STEM board books seem to have more worldly goals. Babies learning about coding and structural engineering are babies getting ready to work.

When I spoke with Peg Oliveira, the director of the Gesell Program in Early Childhood at the Yale Child Study Center, she called these books “a PowerPoint presentation dressed up as a board book.” But Oliveira thinks their deficiencies go beyond that. “The whole goal of board books is to build preliteracy skills,” she said, “introducing babies and toddlers to the idea that books are fun and reading is pleasurable. What do babies learn from a board book about electromagnetics? That books are boring and reading is hard.”

“We expect children to clear academic hurdles at younger and younger ages—counting by preschool, reading by kindergarten,” Oliveira went on. And now, apparently, quantum physics by toddlerhood. The capabilities that children require to succeed in the world are both more basic and more sophisticated than what these books offer: things like problem-solving, curiosity, creativity, and perseverance.

As Oliveira described it, reading with babies is a process of “serve and return, like in a game of tennis: the parent offers something and the child responds, keeping the game going.” When thinking about material for children, she said, “You want to ask, Does it meet the developmental needs of the child now, and does it support them in trying out the next stage of development?” Does it push the child to grow? “We learn like going up stairs,” she said. “We need some help, some stability before we take the next step.” This framework for early literacy underscores why it’s so important for board books to offer familiar language and simple story lines. During the crucial period before the age of three, infants and toddlers are building the skills that will eventually turn them into readers: first, they learn to understand individual words, then to recite lines from their favorite books, then to grasp the rudiments of stories and to create their own.

To Oliveira, a good board book has “words that are fun in your mouth”—a text bolstered by rhyme, rhythm, and repetition—along with bright, high-contrast pictures of things a baby can name. By these metrics, board books that shine include Bruce Degen’s “Jamberry,” Margaret Wise Brown’s “Goodnight Moon,” and the entire Sandra Boynton œuvre. It seems almost unfair to compare lines like “Quickberry! Quackberry! Pick me a blackberry!”(from “Jamberry”) and “Rhinoceroses SNORT and SNUFF and little dogs go RUFF RUFF RUFF!” (from “Moo, Baa, La La La”) with the eye-glazing statement “Everything in the world is made of atoms and molecules” (from “Baby Loves Quarks!”).

Infants and toddlers are unique end users, since they can’t choose, buy, or rate the product themselves. But reports from parents and caregivers can give us an idea. Another librarian I met, Nora Reilly, of Sandy Hook, Connecticut, purchased several Spiro books for her grandson. “He liked them when he was about nine months old,” she said. “I think he was attracted to the illustrations of the baby’s faces, especially the eyes. But, after he turned one, the books didn’t hold his attention.” In other words, at just the age when a child can recognize familiar objects based on the words being read aloud, the science jargon made the books inaccessible: their language became a barrier rather than a gateway to understanding.

Kate Sheblak, a parent of a twenty-month-old in Green Bay, Wisconsin, owns five of the “Baby Loves Science” titles. The enthusiasm that her daughter, Elliott, showed for the books peaked at around twelve to fifteen months, Sheblak told me, but she saw more value in the series than Reilly did. “Elliott liked the simple illustrations,” she said. “The thermodynamics one has a kitty, baby, and sun that she could point to and name.” Both Sheblak and her husband have technical backgrounds, and they found that “some of the analogies the books use don’t make a ton of sense.” Still, she added, “My mom was very big on ‘You can’t read too many books to a baby.’ ”

As long as these STEM board books occupy just one sliver of a baby’s home library, it’s hard to argue with that wisdom. And, if the books get tech-oriented parents into the habit of reading to their kids, so much the better. Between 2008 and 2024, the number of computer-science majors in the U.S. rose fivefold, a trend that suggests a similarly sharp rise in the number of young parents with tech degrees. Maybe, to these parents, a baby book on coding is more than just a bedtime aid: it allows them to share something they love with someone they love. From that angle, Oliveira doesn’t dispute the books’ value. “If these books keep parents in the game of reading,” she said, “let’s not fault them for that.” ♦

title: Is the Smithsonian Really Trying to Destroy America?
author: @NewYorker
content:
Trump claims that the institution has fallen into the hands of Marxist radicals. A stroll through the exhibitions suggests otherwise.

August 20, 2026

The Immokalee Statue of Liberty in “Many Voices, One Nation,” at the National Museum of American History.Photograph by Lawren Simmons

Earlier this month, when I visited the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History (N.M.A.H.), President Trump’s signage warning of its “ideological capture” had yet to be installed. National Guardsmen marched in the paralyzing heat, which, along with the shadows cast by a revolving sculpture in the courtyard, suggested the eerie calm before the gunfight in a Western. Finally, the silence was broken by laughter—a group of volunteers from Citizen Historians for the Smithsonian, who’d advised me, via text, to look out for “4 old white ladies 🧓🏼🧑🏼‍🦳🧓🏼🧑🏼‍🦳”

“I just think what’s going on is a false narrative,” Deborah Greenbush, a D.C. tour guide who’s taken countless visitors through the museum, said. “I have never once had any adult or youngster express the feeling that what they saw made them feel bad. If it’s factual and actual, we should talk about it.” Next to her were Cindy Stevens, a former public-housing administrator, and Pege Gilgannon, a former photojournalist, who wore a shirt emblazoned with the words “Free D.C.” (She frequently volunteers for the D.C.-statehood movement.) Leading the group was Patti Curtis, a STEM adviser at the Department of Education, who retired just before its DOGE-driven evisceration. “They eliminated the entire research department,” she said. “I’m grateful that the Smithsonian isn’t just rolling over like some of our federal agencies.”

The four women are neighbors, and belong to a nonprofit community for seniors. “It’s your second family,” Gilgannon explained. “So you don’t just sit there playing mah-jongg.” Last summer, Curtis persuaded them to join Citizen Historians, a grassroots effort to monitor Smithsonian exhibitions for political interference. She’d heard about the group from one of its founders, James Millward, a central-Asia scholar at Georgetown. “He said, ‘I’ve taught in China and seen history erased, and I don’t want it to happen here.’ ” Not long before, Trump had pressured the director of the National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, to resign, in part because his official portrait’s wall text mentioned his two impeachments. Curtis organized forty volunteers to photograph its collections; altogether, more than seven hundred people have participated in Citizen Historian campaigns.

Trump’s anti-Smithsonian crusade began in March, 2025, with an executive order called “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” A declaration of war against a “revisionist movement” that saw America as “irredeemably flawed,” the order called for the removal of “improper ideology” from the Smithsonian’s twenty-one museums, and threatened to slash the institution’s funding if it didn’t comply. Soon, there were panicked reports—later debunked—that artifacts from slavery and the civil-rights movement had been quietly removed.

For a year, though, the Smithsonian has been spared, in part because of its semi-independent status. It’s governed by a seventeen-member Board of Regents, which includes the Vice-President, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, six federal lawmakers, and nine congressionally appointed members of the general public. The institution’s secretary, Lonnie G. Bunch III, has defended its integrity, but also shrewdly avoided provocative shows of resistance. Last August, he reportedly charmed Trump over lunch at the White House, and by the start of this summer’s Semiquincentennial celebrations, it was almost possible to believe that the Administration had moved on. Then, on July 4th, the White House Domestic Policy Council published a report called “Saving America’s Story,” which alleges that the N.M.A.H. has been hijacked by a cohort of radical activists. Shortly thereafter, Trump ordered the National Park Service to install warning signs outside the museum, whose director, Anthea Hartig, was summoned to testify on Capitol Hill.

“I was disturbed to hear about the quetzal,” Morgan Griffith, a congressman from Virginia, told Hartig, alluding to the suspiciously foreign bird feathers in a children’s show about money. (Quetzal feathers were once used as currency by the Aztecs and their trading partners in the American Southwest.) Nancy Mace, of South Carolina, called Hartig an ally of “queer pedophiles,” adducing, as evidence, a photo of RuPaul from an exhibition on American pop culture. Republicans also played a montage of Hartig making land acknowledgments, demanded to know why she’d once said that “loving America is very complicated,” and expressed outrage that no special exhibitions had been mounted about the Founding Fathers or the Declaration of Independence.

Democrats denounced the proceedings as a totalitarian show trial. Their star witness, the Pulitzer-winning historian David W. Blight, called the White House report “a declaration of political war on the historian’s profession,” and scoffed at accusations of left-wing revisionism. “All history is revision,” he said. “Would you prefer your doctors not to be revisionists?” Hartig, by contrast, was polite almost to the point of meekness, constrained by her role to “Sir”ing and “Ma’am”ing her inquisitors while affirming her commitment to a patriotism that was “not instructed but inspired.” She invited lawmakers to “walk the building with me” and “stand in front of the Star-Spangled Banner, in awe”—implying, not without reason, that many had never even visited the museum they were so determined to control.

If they did come, the Citizen Historians were determined to get there first. Curtis unfolded a map of the museum with eight galleries circled in hot pink. “We powwowed last night and realized we could hit four of them,” she explained. “Rather than split up, let’s go together and saturate.”

“Can anybody read that?” Gilgannon whispered, holding her phone up like a flashlight.

“Yeah, ‘Oh say can you see by the dawn’s early light,’ ” Curtis replied.

We were standing in the darkened chamber that houses the Star-Spangled Banner, whose tattered stripes were dimly visible behind glass. The flag was made by Mary Pickersgill, who sewed it with the help of her daughter, two nieces, and an “African-American indentured servant” named Grace Wisher. Curtis frowned. “Do we really think she was an ‘indentured servant’?” she asked, wondering if the label had originally read “slave.” Gilgannon sighed: “I hate how they put it in your head that you’re gonna get tricked.”

The White House report contends that N.M.A.H. has abandoned patriotism and erased the Founding Fathers in service of an “anti-white agenda” that seeks to “divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens.” But a quick search of the collections database revealed that nearly a hundred objects associated with George Washington and the Revolutionary War—including Washington’s uniform, his battle sword, and his dinner plates—were on display. From the Star-Spangled Banner, we made our way to Horatio Greenough’s 1841 sculpture of a shirtless, sword-bearing Washington, its caption explaining how the sculptor had captured his “highest and noblest virtues.” Greenbush, the tour guide, was amused by his neoclassically bare chest. “He would have been mortified, I’m sure.”

Behind Washington was “Many Voices, One Nation,” an exhibition about the struggle of disparate peoples to forge an American identity. A video collage showcasing America’s diversity played on loop near the entrance; Gilgannon, whose family comes from Belgium, said, “My mother’s in there.” The four women fanned out to photograph the objects on display: an Irish brooch, a Chinese-American shop sign, a collection of accessories abandoned by migrants in the Sonoran Desert. The report frames the show as “pro-illegal alien activism,” but hadn’t mentioned its Border Patrol uniform, whose caption praised the agent’s twenty-two years of service. Later, we gawked at the lavishly decorated 1963 Chevy Impala in “Corazón y vida,” another exhibit derided as a paean to “foreign” peoples—the Chicanos of Southern California, who started building “lowriders” with elaborate hydraulic systems in the nineteen-forties. “I think I’d be scared when it lifts up,” Curtis said, inspecting the undercarriage. “We went to see ‘The Odyssey’ in 4DX a few weeks ago and I was screaming!”

On the top floor was “American Democracy,” a sweeping exhibition about self-governance. Near the entrance was the desk where Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence. Farther in was paraphernalia from a quarter millennium of Presidential campaigns, including Trump’s. (There was even a MAGA hat.) The exhibition culminated in a display of protest signs. The report characterizes them as “almost all for various progressive causes,” and I quickly spotted slogans familiar from Black Lives Matter and the campaign for marriage equality. But equally prominent were “Secure Our Borders,” “Stop Abortion Now,” and projected footage from a Tea Party rally—all unmentioned. Gilgannon took a picture of one from the D.C.-statehood movement. “They practice and promote joy,” she explained. “At first, I thought, What’s this crazy woo-woo? But that’s what’s going to bond us together when we have to, like, fight the National Guard.”

There was plenty of joy in “Entertainment Nation,” a bright, busy, and noisily media-rich survey of American pop culture. Greeting visitors was a photo of the jazz trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, a “cool, Cold Warrior” who used music to fight Communism. Nearby was the sheet music for Irving Berlin’s “God Bless America” and Dorothy’s ruby slippers from “The Wizard of Oz,” whose L.G.B.T.Q. affiliations somehow escaped Republican scrutiny. It took several minutes for Greenbush and me to find the exhibition’s most controversial inclusion—an animation sketch depicting Mickey Mouse’s début in “Steamboat Willie” (1928), whose caption links the character to “longstanding traditions of blackface minstrelsy.” For once, a Citizen Historian and the report were on the same side. “Who would even make that connection?” Greenbush scoffed. “Maybe I’m naïve, but I never would have thought that. And there were points where I did watch a lot of Mickey Mouse.”

During the hearings, Representative Brandon Gill, of Texas, asked Hartig a question precision-engineered to extract a disqualifying sound bite: “Is Mickey Mouse racist?” When she said no, Gill quoted the caption—and again, Hartig affirmed Mickey’s innocence. “You don’t think blackface minstrelsy is racist?” Gill asked, now genuinely confused. Hartig kept calm. “It’s not for me to determine what’s problematic,” she replied. “It’s for me to determine what’s accurate.”

It’s well established that the Mickey Mouse of “Steamboat Willie”—who wears white gloves and performs the minstrel standard “Turkey in the Straw” on a paddle steamer—has its roots in blackface, which was, for nearly a century, one of America’s most popular forms of entertainment. To Republican lawmakers, pointing this out is character assassination, an attempt to cancel poor Mickey and all who hold him dear. But if Representative Gill visited the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American Culture, he might be surprised to learn how many great Black entertainers—including Eubie Blake and Josephine Baker—share Mickey’s checkered beginnings, and with what impartial curiosity these are explored.

Our tour of “Entertainment Nation” concluded with a video installation called “What’s So Funny?” It juxtaposed racist moments in old films and cartoons—Judy Garland dancing in blackface, Bugs Bunny fighting the Indian Wars—with excerpts from the routines of nonwhite comedians such as Margaret Cho and Richard Pryor. We laughed and cringed by turns, our faces painted by the light from the projectors. The 1946 film “Song of the South” came on, and I could feel us all torn between humming along to “Zip-A-Dee-Do-Dah”—a song that my grandmother, a Black woman, loves enough that she once bought an alarm clock with the melody—and recoiling in shame from Uncle Remus’s toothy grin. “My grandfather was actually in minstrel shows,” Greenbush abruptly volunteered. And yet, there she was, protecting our messy common heritage from being wiped clean.

How did the Smithsonian commemorate American history in simpler times, before postmodernism, intersectionality, and the many other Hydra heads of “woke”? The museum’s Semiquincentennial exhibitions struck me as neutral enough. But in order to assess their patriotism objectively, I needed to see how the N.M.A.H. had marked the 1976 Bicentennial, when the museum, the Smithsonian, and the federal government were all helmed by white men.

To my surprise, there was nary an exhibition dedicated to a Founding Father. But there had been a monumental show called “The Nation of Nations,” whose subject was America’s diversity. It opened with a survey of Native cultures, tracing the country’s identity as a “nation of immigrants” to the first Siberians who crossed the Bering Strait. A display about Ellis Island—which played recordings in dozens of languages—celebrated modern immigration, while a re-created nineteenth-century classroom was used to explain the process of naturalization. An entire section dedicated to American prejudice included anti-Japanese signage and a Ku Klux Klan hood.

Curators seem not to have worried that this would divide the American people. In the exhibition catalogue, then secretary of the Smithsonian S. Dillon Ripley—a former intelligence officer who was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by Ronald Reagan—describes America as “a place of turmoil among red men, white men, black men, and yellow men.” Yet no one hauled him before Congress to answer for stoking racial tensions, snubbing George Washington, or making America sad on her birthday. Today’s Smithsonian should be equally uncontroversial—and, without the Trump Administration’s propaganda, it probably would be.

The institution remains vulnerable. Republicans have proposed cutting its budget by more than ten per cent, and if they can fill the vacancies on its Board of Regents before the midterm elections, they may be able to fire Bunch. Yet there are also signs that the right’s revisionism panic might be petering out. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska recently came out in support of the Smithsonian, while the Second Lady, Usha Vance, even feels comfortable collaborating with it. In May, she led a story-time event at the N.M.A.H. in honor of Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month—in other words, a D.E.I. event for children, at a museum that her party believes is full of “inappropriate sexual and ideological content.” (She read from “Masala Chai, Fast and Slow,” by Rajani LaRocca, who is also known for “Some of Us,” a book for early readers that celebrates immigrant citizenship.)

She’s not the only conservative who didn’t get the memo. The day after my visit to the N.M.A.H., I went to see “America’s Presidents” at the National Portrait Gallery, where I found a father and son snapping selfies in front of Trump’s glowering mien. “We wanted to have a last weekend together before he went off to college,” the man explained; earlier, they’d been to the National Air and Space Museum. The man proudly acknowledged supporting Trump, but seemed confused when I asked if he’d spotted anything “radical.” He recalled a caption about a “wealthy landowner back in the day” who’d enslaved Native Americans, which he wasn’t sure was relevant, but he wouldn’t go so far as to say that it ought to be removed. “I don’t know if it’s unpatriotic,” he said. “It’s all good and bad. It’s part of our history.” ♦

Julian Lucas, a staff writer, began contributing to The New Yorker in 2018.

title: Thank This Retired Projectionist for Those 3 a.m. Odyssey 70-mm. Imax Showings
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
Pat Caldwell is 69 years old and, as Chris Stanton gushes in this uproarious Q&A, “a legend to IMAX nerds.” Caldwell loves Vision3 film stock, hates Joker: Folie à Deux, and has discovered more than one dead body in a movie theater. His decades-long career as a projectionist includes a stint at a Tennessee porn theater with “very good equipment,” and he once spent half a year screening Lawrence of Arabia four times daily. When Stanton reached out to Caldwell on the occasion of The Odyssey, he may have landed the year’s most entertaining interview.

So Sam taught me how to run the projectors, and he got drunk, passed out on the couch. And after the concession stand in the box office closed, I would go up and run the rest of the movies for him. This went very nicely until one night there’s a knock at the door. I opened the door and here’s this old man standing there. And I said, “Well, who are you?” He says, “I could ask the same question. Who are you? I’m the business agent of the local projectionists’ union.” I explained what was going on. He woke up Sam, chewed him out. And the next day they made me an apprentice. I trained for a year with no pay at all the local theaters in Nashville.

title: Why Millennial Professionals Are Embracing Socialism
author: @NewYorker
content:
During the past few weeks, I’ve heard from a lot of readers who have theories about Subaru Socialists, the term I used, in a recent column, to refer to middle-class, college-educated, liberal millennials. Some of the critics of this cohort blame colleges for pushing left-wing politics and engendering an excess of concern for struggling people; more sympathetic readers credit the work of community organizing and activism for generating those very same things. Reading these reactions has pushed me to consider a subset of the Subaru Socialists: professionals in their thirties and forties who are now basically doing fine financially, and may even belong to the upper middle class. It used to be a cliché that youthful idealism eventually gives way to fiscal conservatism (and to thinking way more than you ever expected you would about your taxes). How did this group veer away from that once seemingly inevitable trajectory?

A little self-reflection might be in order. Like many of my Subaru Socialist ilk, I went into debt for an arguably useless graduate degree—a Master of Fine Arts in fiction, from Columbia. After finishing that degree, I spent several years getting rejected by pretty much every publishing house and magazine there is. When the Great Recession happened, I was twenty-eight, and I lost my job as a private-school teacher, leading to an extended stay on unemployment. All of this felt bad, but I didn’t really channel it into the politics of the left until Bernie Sanders began showing up on campaign stages, in 2015. By then, I had paid off my student loans, had bought a home, and was making enough money as a writer that I no longer needed to feverishly check my account balances or worry too much about buying a plane ticket or new car parts.

As I have thought more about others like me—comfortable people in their forties who are nonetheless frustrated enough with capitalism and the Democratic establishment to vote for seemingly any insurgent candidate in sight—I’ve wondered why I started thinking seriously about universal health care, wealth redistribution, and the expansion of the public sector at the precise moment that I didn’t really need them anymore. An obvious answer would be that it’s hard to think very much about politics when you’re struggling to get your bank account consistently above five hundred dollars. But I find that unconvincing—even when things were bad, I wasn’t entirely immiserated, and I still read the news. I also can’t plead ignorance: I had a Marxist phase in college and spent my early twenties talking solemnly about revolutions and the proletariat. But those convictions were abstract, if sincere, and I suppose they stayed that way until Sanders came along.

What—or, rather, who—bridged my youthful communism and the softer populist politics of my thirties and forties? Barack Obama. I remember the excitement I felt after Obama’s victory in 2008 not as one recalls a moment in history that locks you into a time and a generation but more as something that happened to me, personally, like hitting a buzzer beater in a basketball game or going on a first date. Until the full reality of the financial crash and its aftermath set in, Obama and his great hope of multiethnic progress put my youthful questions about wealth inequality and the crimes of Wall Street at bay. I believed, as so many of us did, that we would all just float up to an era of prosperity and racial harmony. By the time Sanders came around, that vague hope had curdled into resentment. I wanted nothing to do with anti-racist, neoliberal corporate politics—during this time I took to stringing such terms together—even if I understood that they were probably good for me and my career, perhaps more so than tax policies that favored the upper middle class.

I should note that I do not think that Obama’s Presidency was a great failure; nor do I believe that Obama sold out the millions of acolytes who, upon seeing him take the stage at the Democratic National Convention in 2004 and deliver his “skinny kid with a funny name” speech, treated him like a saint. But his handling of the financial crash ultimately forced many of us to acknowledge that the floaty dream was over and that he had not delivered. An alternative was needed, one that felt bound both to a personality and to an idea. We didn’t know exactly who that alternative might be—even as Sanders gained momentum following his shocking win in the Michigan primary—but we knew, right away, who it was not: Hillary Clinton.

Subaru Socialism grew, in part, out of the 2008 crash, the subsequent disappointment in Obama, and a rejection of Clinton and her entitled, uninviting run at the Presidency. But why did it take the shape it did? Why the socialist bent? Couldn’t these same factors have led to a more centrist politics focussed on the repudiation of Donald Trump and on a celebration of free markets that could lift up new immigrants into a strong middle class?

There are multiple reasons. One is the cultural and political celebrity of Sanders. Also, our politics sometimes lags behind our economic reality. The first Sanders campaign made me realize that I did get kinda screwed on my student loans, and that things maybe shouldn’t have been so hard. I felt retrospective anger toward Columbia for offering a program that charged people fifty thousand dollars a year, guaranteed absolutely nothing in return, and seemed unconcerned with the debt that many of its students were piling up. Friends of mine from that program never recovered financially. I also came to appreciate the safety net provided by California’s unemployment benefits, which allowed me to figure out what I could do next—the 2008 crash didn’t doom me to eviction and starting over at my parents’ house (even if I eventually ended up there for a short time).

More than any of this, though, I felt inspired by Sanders’s universalist message, and by his refusal to participate in the factional, identity-based battles that I had long suspected served only as a kind of promotional package for the careers of politicians, academics, and corporate employees. This was part of the disappointment with Obama, too—the realization that even if more “people of color” moved up the corporate and political ladders, we would simply end up with a slightly more diverse ruling class.

Sometimes, politics takes root not at the point of misery, but years later, when the agita has passed and someone can explain why it had to be that way. It took me a few years to fully get on board with the left. The hope that Obama inspired in me died a bit more slowly than one might expect, in no small part because I am a minority and therefore especially attached to the idea of a prosperous, post-racial America. When I had children, though, I found myself moving further toward broad, fuzzy support for anything semi-socialist. My wife and I could afford child care, but we could also see just how little would have to change to make that impossible. And during the first Trump Presidency it became quite obvious to me that, although I had somehow become more successful as a writer than I ever could have imagined during my days of unemployment and rejection, the job was shakier and less stable than it would have been not that long before.

You could say the same about many jobs, particularly those in fields where you’re likely to find a lot of Subaru Socialists: academia, the arts, the entertainment industry, even advertising. All of these fields tend to require quite a bit of school and have far less stability than they once did. And people in these fields have done much to shape the thinking of their peers. Will Menaker, one of the hosts of the influential leftist podcast “Chapo Trap House,” is the son of Daniel Menaker, a longtime fiction editor at this magazine who later became the executive editor-in-chief of Random House. Will made a go of it in his father’s industry before becoming one of the most biting and incisive voices of the so-called Bernie Bro movement. His experience is particular and, as he freely admits, extremely privileged, but it’s also exemplary, to some degree. I listened to almost every episode of “Chapo Trap House” when it first launched, and I recall feeling both put off by Menaker’s culturally élite, private-school background and somewhat connected to him—because he and I were more or less seeing the same thing.

Menaker told me that he and his co-hosts did not set out to embody the anger of the downwardly mobile, middle-class youth, though it did ultimately shake out that way. This makes sense; no podcast or live stream—at least no very good one—started out with such an explicit political goal. But their show, like talk-radio shows of the past, provided a relatable, consistent voice that allowed listeners to see themselves a bit more clearly. One of the key dynamics of the Bernie Bro movement was that, although it talked about the working class, it also showed the previously privileged classes how to proletarianize themselves, in part by asking a simple question: If it sucks for us, how bad must it be for everyone else?

You could look at all this and conclude that Subaru Socialists such as myself are vain, unserious, and fully unsympathetic. After all, nobody made me go to an expensive graduate program—at Columbia, of all places—and it may even seem ungrateful to study at one of the most prestigious institutions on the planet and then get mad when it doesn’t yield what it seemed to promise (especially in my case, since it basically did). Nobody is entitled to work their dream job. But along with more personal disappointments came the realization that the industry I was hoping to enter might never get any healthier, and that this was true in those other fields as well, and many others besides. That forced me to think about my daughter and what protections she would need if, God forbid, she decided to try to become a writer like her father. Would she have health care? Could she ever afford to buy a home? How much wealth would be captured by the tech oligarchy, and how far would she be—despite growing up privileged by any standard—from earning some of that money? How close would she be to ending up in much worse shape than her parents?

Those are my politics of self-interest, and the reasons that the left keeps making sense to me, even as I burrow comfortably into the upper middle class. The children of the Subaru Socialists will almost certainly have it worse than their parents. No matter what sort of privileged and perhaps contradictory path you took to reach that conclusion, once you see it, you can’t look away. ♦

title: Dolphins Eavesdrop on Their Prey—and Each Other
content:
Dolphins are a noisy bunch. They whistle to identify each other and interact socially. And their series of rapid-fire echolocating clicks allow them to feel their way around, acoustically checking out the contours of the underwater landscape and finding prey. These days, however, dolphins have to compete with a ton of different human-made noises, from oil drilling to ship traffic to explosives, that impair their communication. 

Featured Video

Adding to the acoustic melee, a paper recently published in PeerJ found that dolphins may be eavesdropping on fishes that make sound, such as drums (Sciaenidae) that croak by vibrating their swim bladders but are known to become quieter in the presence of dolphin sounds.

Florida Atlantic University researchers with the Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute listened in on dolphins for two months along the Atlantic Coast from Fort Pierce to Jacksonville. A wave glider towed an underwater recording device suspended 4 to 10 meters below the surface, while also measuring currents, depths, and other physical parameters. 

Read more: “What Do Dolphins Talk About?”

In 62 hours of ocean sounds compiled from 15-second recordings every five minutes, dolphins were detected either whistling or echolocating (or both) about 1,700 times. The acoustic data, when crossed with aspects of the physical surroundings, revealed nuances in dolphin sound production. The study paves the way for identifying areas of high acoustic importance to dolphins that should be protected from human noise pollution.

“When we combine dolphin vocalizations with the sounds of their prey and the physical characteristics of the ocean,” explained marine biologist and co-author Greg O-Corry-Crowe in a statement, “we begin to see the underwater environment from the dolphins’ perspective.”

They found that dolphins whistled more when close to shore, varying with water temperature and chlorophyll concentrations, among other factors. Because dolphin whistles may carry 12 miles or more, they’re useful in keeping a group together. Their echolocation clicks, on the other hand, were concentrated in two stretches where sound-producing fish are known to abound, including croakers, toadfish, and carangids. And so, the dolphins may be listening to the croaking and other fish sounds to home in on their prey.

“What we’re seeing is a fascinating separation between the acoustic behaviors dolphins use for social life and those they use for finding food,” said O-Corry-Crowe. “Everybody is snooping on everybody else.”

title: The End of the European Summer
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Europe is warming more than twice as fast as the global average—a terrifying statistic made all too apparent this summer as heat wave followed heat wave. European cities were never designed for these temperatures, and public health, infrastructure, and tourism are all under strain. Eric Klinenberg arrives in Milan just as “Europe’s third heat wave of the summer entered its fiercest stretch” and sweats his way across the continent to see how trees, shade, water, and other measures are being deployed to adapt urban centers. But with this crisis set to deepen can these experiments really keep pace?

Of all the problems that heat poses for Barcelona, losing some of the hundred and sixty thousand tourists who typically visit each day ranks low on the priority lists of most officials and residents. Some locals have staged protests, chanting “Tourists go home” while targeting visitors with water guns. But tourism employs more than a hundred and sixty thousand people in Barcelona and accounts for around thirteen per cent of its economic output, which explains why, despite concerns that the city gets too many visitors, more than seventy per cent of residents consider tourism beneficial. At midday, when I arrived on La Rambla, the city’s most heavily visited and photographed corridor, the street had little shade and surprisingly few people. At La Boqueria market, normally jam-packed at lunchtime, I found my way to a famously busy bar counter and took one of several open seats.
